html:
The Onondaga, people of the hills, are one of the five original nations of the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, in central New York around Onondaga Lake and today's Syracuse. They lived in large palisaded towns of longhouses and farmed maize, beans and squash.

Haudenosaunee tradition places the founding of the confederacy at Onondaga Lake, where the Peacemaker and Hiawatha persuaded the five nations to accept the Great Law of Peace and won over Tadodaho, a feared Onondaga chief. The Onondaga became the keepers of the central council fire, and the Grand Council still meets on their land. Tadodaho remains the title of its chair.

Their neighbours and fellow nations were the Mohawk and Oneida to the east and the Cayuga and Seneca to the west. In the American Revolution the army of the new United States burned Onondaga towns in 1779. New York State then took most of their land in the 1780s and 1790s. The Onondaga Nation keeps a small territory south of Syracuse and still governs itself as a sovereign nation under its traditional chiefs.
